title: The emperor's notebook
hookLine: Marcus wrote in Greek, to himself, often on campaign, and the title "Meditations" came later
last: A LOVE HE THOUGHT WAS WIDE.

lines: YOUR NOTES APP, NOT YOUR POSTS.
A TENT ON THE DANUBE, AROUND 170.
cards: Somebody opens your notes app. Not your posts, your notes. The reminders to yourself.
Be patient with Dad. Stop checking your phone. You're not as tired as you think.
A little embarrassing, and also a truer picture of you than any post.
The emperor of Rome kept notes like that: reminders to himself, in Greek, some of them, it seems, written far from Rome on the Danube frontier, around the year 170.

teach.h: WRITTEN ON CAMPAIGN, BY THE DANUBE.
teach.b: Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from 161 to 180. He spent much of his last decade at war along the Danube frontier, and it's likely that much of his notebook was written there, in camp.

A few headings in the manuscripts seem to place him: one book ends with a note that it was written among the Quadi, a people on the far side of the river, and another reads: at Carnuntum, a Roman fort.
Three things are worth knowing. First, he wrote in Greek, not Latin.

teach.h: IN GREEK, THE LANGUAGE OF PHILOSOPHY.
teach.b: Greek was the language of philosophy, and Marcus had studied the Stoics, among them the former slave Epictetus. Second, he wrote to himself.
The notes scold, remind, encourage and repeat, the way you do when you haven't learned something yet. That's part of why they feel so alive: this isn't a man who has arrived; it's a man practicing.
Third, the well-known title isn't his.

The old manuscripts carry a Greek heading usually translated to himself, and it may have been added by whoever copied the notes after his death. Meditations is what English readers later called the book.
It survived by a thin thread of copies and was first printed in the 1550s. So beside Rumi this camp, remember the difference. Rumi spoke his book aloud to a friend who wrote it down.
Marcus wrote his alone, for no one. Both, somehow, made it through the centuries.

how: Readers of the Meditations often keep it by the bed and read a single short section at a time, and many who follow modern Stoic practice keep their own journal of notes to themselves.

games.q: you're emperor, at war on a cold frontier, and at night you have an hour alone. what do you do with it?
o: write notes to yourself about how to live.
write a history of the war.
games.why: Marcus wrote notes to himself, reminders that scold, encourage and repeat. as far as we can tell, they were meant for no one else.

practice: Ask what you keep needing to remember and keep forgetting: be kinder to your sister, rest is not failure, finish before you start the next thing.
Find one plain, honest sentence, the way you'd say it to a friend, and say it inside, slowly. If you can, write it down somewhere you'll see it again.
